links.title: Logs
links.tooltip: Logs dashboard, carrying the current time range. Variables are not carried — logs filters on log-group tokens (main/test), not the metric `network` label (mainnet/testnet).

list.name: deployment
list.label: Deployment
list.description: Blue/green colour(s) to include. Multi-select; "All" covers both. Has no effect on the Edge rows — CloudFront and WAF sit in front of both colours.

list.name: network
list.label: Network
list.description: VeChain network(s) to include. Values match the `network` external label emitted by the ADOT sidecar (terraform/api/observability.tf network_label map) — `mainnet`/`testnet`, not the `main`/`test` tokens used in log group names. Applies to the Prometheus panels only; the Edge rows are per-network and fixed.

list.name: filters
list.label: Filters
list.description: Ad-hoc label filters applied to every AMP (Prometheus) panel — uri, status, task_id, collection, command, endpoint, … Replaces the old URI textbox. Does not apply to the CloudWatch Edge rows, which are a different datasource.

panels.title: CloudFront requests (total)
panels.description: AWS/CloudFront Requests (Sum) totalled over the dashboard time range, both distributions collapsed into one figure — the graph beside it keeps them apart. The two series are joined and summed per timestamp in transformations because a stat panel otherwise renders one number per series. Period is left on auto so a range past CloudFront's 15-day 1-minute retention rolls up instead of returning nothing. Edge volume, so it sits above the API row's 'Total requests': cache hits and WAF blocks never reach the origin.

panels.title: Cache hit rate (average)
panels.description: AWS/CloudFront CacheHitRate (Average, %) reduced to one figure: the mean of the per-period averages over the dashboard range, across both distributions. Not a request-weighted hit ratio — CloudFront publishes no hit/miss counts — so a quiet period weighs the same as a busy one, and the spare distribution the same as the primary whenever it serves. Read it beside the graph, not instead of it.

panels.title: CloudFront requests
panels.description: AWS/CloudFront Requests (Sum) across the two distributions fronting indexer.mainnet.vechain.org (E15Q64MS368TL primary, E1LMOFNZTMWN6R spare/replica). Fixed to this network and not affected by the Network or Deployment pickers — CloudFront and WAF are shared across both blue/green colours and are not templated. CloudFront metrics are 1-minute granularity and publish with a few minutes of lag, so this trails the Prometheus panels below.

panels.title: Cache hit rate
panels.description: AWS/CloudFront CacheHitRate (Average, %). Higher = more edge hits, less origin load. The indexer API is largely uncacheable so expect low double digits at best; drops toward zero on cache invalidation or a hot-path change.

panels.title: CloudFront error rate — 4xx / 5xx
panels.description: AWS/CloudFront 4xxErrorRate + 5xxErrorRate (Average, %) — percentage of viewer requests returning 4xx/5xx at the edge. Cross-reference with the API panels in the Errors row: edge errors the origin never saw are WAF blocks or CloudFront-level failures.

panels.title: WAF — allowed vs blocked
panels.description: AWS/WAFV2 AllowedRequests + BlockedRequests (Sum, Rule=ALL). Aggregate across the whole shared-veworld-cloudfront-waf WebACL.

panels.title: WAF — blocked requests by rule
panels.description: AWS/WAFV2 BlockedRequests (Sum) split by Rule. Rule = the CloudWatch metric name from VisibilityConfig.MetricName. Spike hunters: rate-based rule (a customer being throttled), block-ip-set (specific IP blocked), block-get-options-swagger (non-GET/OPTIONS request rejected).

panels.title: WAF — counted requests by rule (dry run)
panels.description: AWS/WAFV2 CountedRequests (Sum). A COUNT rule flags a request and lets it through, so this is what a tighter limit would have caught — nothing here was blocked. "High-rate IP dry run" is waf--custom-AWS-count-high-rate-ip, tripping above high_rate_count_limit requests per IP per 5 min with none of the rate-limit exemptions, so the block-explorer proxy egress would be counted too. While no IP crosses the threshold CloudWatch creates no series for it at all, so it is absent from the legend rather than drawn at zero — "All count-mode rules" is the WebACL-wide aggregate, carried here so the panel still renders and proves the query path is alive; the dry-run rule is a subset of it, which is why the series are not stacked. For the flagged IPs and paths use wafv2 get-sampled-requests — get-rate-based-statement-managed-keys stays empty for a count-only rule, since it lists only keys actually being limited.

panels.title: Indexers by sync status
panels.description: count by (status) of indexers where indexer_sync_status == 1. Deduped across task_id — deployment/network are kept in the inner max so a shared indexer_name across networks isn't collapsed — and constrained to the last 45s so post-deploy stale series drop out before the default 5m lookback.

targets.expr: count by (status) (max by (indexer_name, status, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_sync_status{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name", service="indexer"}[45s])) == 1)

panels.title: Sync gap — blocks behind Thor best
panels.description: max(thor_best) − max(indexer_current) per indexer, clamped to ≥ 0 and forced to 0 when the indexer reports FULLY_SYNCED (raw block-number diff can drift 1–3 blocks from sampling timing even when caught up). Bars sorted by gap desc, indexer name asc as tiebreaker; > 100 orange, > 500 red. Bar labels carry the indexer's current mode, joined in from the indexer_sync_status one-hot and shortened for width: label_replace strips the trailing `Indexer`, cuts the colour to its initial, drops `-net` from the network, and maps each status to a short form (FULLY_SYNCED → synced, FAST_SYNCING → fast, NOT_INITIALISED → uninit, and so on).

panels.title: Time to fully synced — at the current rate
panels.description: Sync gap divided by the rate the gap is closing: the fastest 5-minute throughput in the last half hour, max_over_time(rate(indexer_blocks_processed_total[5m])[30m:1m]), minus the chain's own growth, deriv(thor_best_block_number[30m]). Peak rather than average because the counter only advances while an indexer is SYNCING, FAST_SYNCING or FULLY_SYNCED — a 30-minute average divides a fresh sync's blocks by the idle stretch before it and reads far too high until that window clears. A READY_TO_SYNC or READY_TO_FAST_SYNC indexer has processed nothing since it started, usually because it is yoked into a proximity group behind a slower member, so its own rate is zero or absent; it shows the slowest SYNCING/FAST_SYNCING estimate on its network instead, which is when that group reaches the head. A SYNCING indexer idling behind its group still holds its last rate for 30 minutes and reads optimistically. A fast-syncing indexer runs an order of magnitude faster than the live loop, so its estimate drops sharply the moment it leaves FAST_SYNCING; read the mode in the bar label before believing a jump. FULLY_SYNCED indexers are pinned to 0 the same way the gap panel pins them, and the bar labels are built the same way.

targets.expr: label_replace(label_replace(label_replace((((max by (deployment, network) (clamp_min((max by (deployment, network) (thor_best_block_number{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}) - on(deployment, network) group_right() max by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (indexer_current_block{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"})) * on(deployment, network, indexer_name) group_left() (1 - max by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (indexer_sync_status{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", status="FULLY_SYNCED", service="indexer"})), 0) / clamp_min(max_over_time(sum by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (rate(indexer_blocks_processed_total{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}[5m]))[30m:1m]) - on(deployment, network) group_left() clamp_min(max by (deployment, network) (deriv(thor_best_block_number{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}[30m])), 0), 0.001) * on(deployment, network, indexer_name) group_left() (max by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (last_over_time(indexer_sync_status{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", status=~"SYNCING|FAST_SYNCING", service="indexer"}[45s])) == 1))) * on(deployment, network) group_right() (max by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (last_over_time(indexer_sync_status{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name", status=~"READY_TO_SYNC|READY_TO_FAST_SYNC", service="indexer"}[45s])) == 1)) or clamp_min((max by (deployment, network) (thor_best_block_number{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}) - on(deployment, network) group_right() max by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (indexer_current_block{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name", service="indexer"})) * on(deployment, network, indexer_name) group_left() (1 - max by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (indexer_sync_status{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name", status="FULLY_SYNCED", service="indexer"})), 0) / clamp_min(max_over_time(sum by (deployment, network, indexer_name) (rate(indexer_blocks_processed_total{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name", service="indexer"}[5m]))[30m:1m]) - on(deployment, network) group_left() clamp_min(max by (deployment, network) (deriv(thor_best_block_number{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}[30m])), 0), 0.001)) * on (deployment, network, indexer_name) group_left(status) label_replace(label_replace(label_replace(label_replace(label_replace(label_replace(label_replace((max by (deployment, network, indexer_name, status) (last_over_time(indexer_sync_status{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name", service="indexer"}[45s])) == 1), "status", "synced", "status", "FULLY_SYNCED"), "status", "syncing", "status", "SYNCING"), "status", "fast", "status", "FAST_SYNCING"), "status", "ready", "status", "READY_TO_SYNC"), "status", "ready/fast", "status", "READY_TO_FAST_SYNC"), "status", "uninit", "status", "NOT_INITIALISED"), "status", "down", "status", "SHUT_DOWN"), "indexer_name", "$1", "indexer_name", "(.*)Indexer"), "deployment", "$1", "deployment", "(.).*"), "network", "$1", "network", "(.*)net")

panels.title: Blocks / sec
panels.description: rate(indexer_blocks_processed_total[1m]) per indexer.

targets.expr: sum by (indexer_name) (rate(indexer_blocks_processed_total{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name"}[1m]))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (indexer_name, le) (rate(processor_duration_seconds_bucket{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", indexer_name=~"$indexer_name"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (endpoint, le) (rate(thor_client_request_duration_seconds_bucket{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m])))

panels.title: API indexes · dropped while an indexer catches up
Indexes waiting to be created
panels.description: How many indexes the API needs are not in the database right now. An indexer that is far behind the chain drops the indexes only the API reads, because maintaining them slows its catch-up down; it rebuilds them when it reaches the head. A number above zero is normal during a resync and should fall back to zero on its own. Until it does, API queries that would use those indexes are slow.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (max by (schema, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_deferrable_indexes_declared{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}[45s]))) - sum by (deployment, network) (max by (schema, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_deferrable_indexes_standing{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}[45s])))

panels.title: Indexers by index state
panels.description: Where each indexer stands on the indexes only the API reads. Present: every one of them exists, which is the normal state. Dropped: the indexer is far enough behind the chain that it has dropped them to catch up faster. Rebuilding: it has reached the head and is putting them back, which stops it taking new blocks until it finishes.

targets.expr: count(max by (schema, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_backfill_phase{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer", phase="SERVING"}[45s])) == 1)
count(max by (schema, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_backfill_phase{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer", phase="BACKFILL"}[45s])) == 1)
count(max by (schema, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_backfill_phase{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer", phase="BUILDING"}[45s])) == 1)

panels.title: Indexes still to create, by indexer
panels.description: Every indexer, ordered by how many indexes it still has to create, so the ones with work sit at the top and the rest read as a tail of zeros. A bar falls one index at a time as a rebuild works through them, and reaching zero is what lets that indexer start taking blocks again.

targets.expr: label_replace(label_replace(label_replace((max by (indexer, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_deferrable_indexes_declared{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}[45s])) - max by (indexer, deployment, network) (last_over_time(indexer_deferrable_indexes_standing{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="indexer"}[45s]))), "indexer", "$1", "indexer", "(.*)Indexer"), "deployment", "$1", "deployment", "(.).*"), "network", "$1", "network", "(.*)net")

panels.title: Total requests
panels.description: Every request the API served over the dashboard time range — the denominator the two topk panels beside it hide. `increase()` is summed per step rather than taken over `$__range` in one shot so the sparkline has a shape; the step is floored at 1m because the sidecar scrapes at 15s and a shorter window can hold too few samples for `increase()` to return anything. Counts what reached the API, so it sits below the Edge row's 'CloudFront requests': cache hits and WAF blocks never arrive here.

targets.expr: sum(increase(http_server_requests_seconds_count{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api"}[$__interval]))

panels.title: Top URIs by total origin time
panels.description: topk(15) of sum by (uri) (increase(http_server_requests_seconds_sum[$__range])) — total seconds of server time each endpoint consumed over the dashboard time range, i.e. request count × mean latency. This is the panel to act on: an endpoint can be the busiest by count and cost almost nothing here (the usual shape for cheap per-user lookups), while a low-volume endpoint with a slow query can dominate. Pair with 'API — avg latency by URI' to see which of the two factors drives a bar.

targets.expr: topk(15, sum by (uri) (increase(http_server_requests_seconds_sum{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api"}[$__range])))

panels.title: Top URIs by total requests
panels.description: topk(15) of sum by (uri) (increase(http_server_requests_seconds_count[$__range])) — absolute request counts over the dashboard time range, not a rate, so bursty and steady traffic are comparable. Ranks by count, not by cost: a path can top this panel and still be near-free, so check 'Top URIs by total origin time' before acting on a bar here. `/**` is Spring's catch-all pattern: every request whose path matched no controller mapping, i.e. all unmatched-path 404s aggregated into one bar. The `uri` label is the matched Spring pattern with the query string stripped, so every parameter shape of one endpoint shares a bar. Full paths and query strings come from the ALB access logs in S3 (prod-{blue,green}-veworld-{main,test}-api-ecs-lb-bucket, prefix veworld-lb/). The mainnet WAF log group logs BLOCKed requests only (logging_filter_block_only), so it is not a traffic census; testnet's logs everything.

targets.expr: topk(15, sum by (uri) (increase(http_server_requests_seconds_count{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api"}[$__range])))

panels.title: API — avg latency by URI
panels.description: rate(sum) / rate(count). Real p95 needs percentile histograms enabled server-side (management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true).

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_sum{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api"}[5m])) / sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api"}[5m])))

panels.title: Requests by X-Project-Id
panels.description: sum by (project) of api_requests_by_project_total increases over the dashboard time range. `unknown` = header missing; `other` = header set but not on the KNOWN_PROJECT_IDS whitelist (raw value logged); the rest are known callers.

targets.expr: sum by (project) (increase(api_requests_by_project_total{service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[$__range]))

panels.title: Top URIs by rate
panels.description: topk(10) of request rate by uri, ranked per timestamp — a URI that goes quiet drops out of the top 10, so its line breaks into a gap rather than sitting at zero. Legend shows Max/Last only: Mean would average the bursts and ignore the gaps, which reads ~20x too high on spiky series like `/**`. For volume use 'Top URIs by total requests'. Narrow to a single endpoint with the Filters bar at the top (uri = …).

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api"}[5m])))
sum by (uri, status) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api", outcome="SERVER_ERROR"}[5m]))
sum by (uri, status) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service="api", outcome="CLIENT_ERROR"}[5m]))
sum by (endpoint, code) (rate(thor_client_response_codes_total{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", code=~"5.."}[5m]))
sum by (endpoint, code) (rate(thor_client_response_codes_total{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", code=~"4.."}[5m]))

panels.title: CPU utilised — per task
panels.description: ecs_task_cpu_utilized / ecs_task_cpu_reserved × 100 for indexer + api. Dashed line = 80%.

targets.expr: (ecs_task_cpu_utilized_None{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service=~"indexer|api"} / ecs_task_cpu_reserved_None{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service=~"indexer|api"}) * 100

panels.title: Memory utilised — per task
panels.description: ecs_task_memory_utilized / ecs_task_memory_reserved × 100 for indexer + api. Dashed line = 80%.

targets.expr: (ecs_task_memory_utilized_Megabytes{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service=~"indexer|api"} / ecs_task_memory_reserved_Megabytes{deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network", service=~"indexer|api"}) * 100

panels.title: API tasks running against desired
panels.description: A gap that outlasts a rolling deploy is a stuck deploy or a placement failure; the `*-api-tasks-below-desired` alarm fires on the same two metrics. API services only: the indexers deploy at deployment_minimum_healthy_percent = 0, so a rolling replacement legitimately sits at zero running tasks for minutes and a gap there says nothing. Service-level counts come from ECS itself, so a dead task reads as a drop to zero — the ADOT per-task series behind the two panels beside it just go absent instead. CloudWatch dimensions cannot be templated, so both colours and both networks are hardcoded here and neither picker applies.

panels.title: Pool size vs active
panels.description: hikaricp_connections vs hikaricp_connections_active for the Postgres pool. Sustained active ≈ size means the pool is saturated — bump postgres.pool.maximum-size or fix a slow query.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (hikaricp_connections{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"})
sum by (deployment, network) (hikaricp_connections_active{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"})

panels.title: Threads waiting for a connection
panels.description: hikaricp_connections_pending — callers blocked on the pool. Anything > 0 sustained surfaces as latency.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (hikaricp_connections_pending{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"})

panels.title: Connection timeouts
panels.description: rate(hikaricp_connections_timeout_total[5m]) — callers that gave up waiting for a connection. Should be zero.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_timeout_total{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))

panels.title: Connection acquire — avg and max
panels.description: hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds: time to get a connection from the pool. Grows before pending does.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_sum{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m])) / sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_count{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))
max by (deployment, network) (max_over_time(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_max{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))

panels.title: Connection usage — avg and max
panels.description: hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds: how long a connection is held, i.e. statement plus commit time.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds_sum{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m])) / sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds_count{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))
max by (deployment, network) (max_over_time(hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds_max{pool="postgres", service="indexer", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))

panels.title: Pool size vs active
panels.description: hikaricp_connections vs hikaricp_connections_active for the Postgres pool. Sustained active ≈ size means the pool is saturated — bump postgres.pool.maximum-size or fix a slow query.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (hikaricp_connections{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"})
sum by (deployment, network) (hikaricp_connections_active{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"})

panels.title: Threads waiting for a connection
panels.description: hikaricp_connections_pending — callers blocked on the pool. Anything > 0 sustained surfaces as latency.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (hikaricp_connections_pending{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"})

panels.title: Connection timeouts
panels.description: rate(hikaricp_connections_timeout_total[5m]) — callers that gave up waiting for a connection. Should be zero.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_timeout_total{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))

panels.title: Connection acquire — avg and max
panels.description: hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds: time to get a connection from the pool. Grows before pending does.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_sum{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m])) / sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_count{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))
max by (deployment, network) (max_over_time(hikaricp_connections_acquire_seconds_max{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))

panels.title: Connection usage — avg and max
panels.description: hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds: how long a connection is held, i.e. statement plus commit time.

targets.expr: sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds_sum{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m])) / sum by (deployment, network) (rate(hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds_count{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))
max by (deployment, network) (max_over_time(hikaricp_connections_usage_seconds_max{pool="postgres", service="api", deployment=~"$deployment", network=~"$network"}[5m]))

panels.title: Newest restorable backup
panels.description: Age of the newest automated snapshot in `available` state, per instance — what restore_dead_prod_pg_snapshots.sh would pick for a dead colour. This is NOT how long ago a backup started: a snapshot is not restorable until it finishes, and mainnet's take hours, so this peaks at roughly 25h plus the run time and drops when the run completes. 'Backup age' below separates the two. Red at 48h is the pg-backup-stale alarm in terraform/api/alarms.tf.

panels.title: Backups retained
panels.description: Available automated snapshots per instance. backup_retention_period is 3 days, so a steady state is 3 or 4. A number that falls and stays down means backups stopped before the retention window emptied. Manual snapshots are deliberately excluded — they are not what a restore selects — but they do appear in the table below.

panels.title: Last backup duration
panels.description: Wall time between the `Backing up DB instance` and `Finished DB Instance backup` events, which is the only completion signal RDS gives — a snapshot carries a start time and no end time. Mainnet currently runs for hours, which is why neither backup alarm is threshold-ed on completion. Only a run that produced an automated snapshot counts, so a manual one such as the destroy workflow's final snapshot is left out; once that snapshot ages out of retention the run reports nothing here.

panels.title: Backup age — started, restorable, oldest
panels.description: Three lines per instance, and the gap between the first two is the point of the panel. `started` is how long ago RDS last began a snapshot, counting one still running — it drops to zero daily no matter how slow the backup is, and is what the pg-backup-not-starting alarm reads. `restorable` only moves when a run finishes, so it trails `started` by the run time. `oldest` is the far edge of the restore window, normally flat at ~3 days. All three climbing together means backups have stopped and the window is ageing out.

panels.title: Backup in progress
panels.description: PercentProgress of any automated snapshot in `creating`, sampled every 5 minutes, with a closing 100 published from the backup finish event — RDS flips a snapshot to `available` without ever reporting 100 itself. Empty is the normal state between runs. Because mainnet backups run for hours this is the panel that shows one actually moving — a line that stops climbing and never reaches 100 is a stuck run, which no alarm catches until 'Newest restorable backup' crosses 48h.

panels.title: Backup duration
panels.description: How long each daily backup took, from the paired RDS backup events. The value is republished on every 5-minute poll until the next backup finishes, so the line is a step, not a sample per backup — read the step changes. Backup time tracks changed blocks since the last snapshot, so a jump usually follows a resync or a bulk rewrite.

panels.title: Volume covered by the newest backup
panels.description: AllocatedStorage of the newest automated snapshot — the size of the volume it covers, which is as close to a backup size as RDS will give. It is NOT the bytes the snapshot consumes: the API exposes no per-snapshot size, the first snapshot of an instance is a full copy and the rest are incremental, and the three AWS/RDS backup-storage metrics (TotalBackupStorageBilled, BackupRetentionPeriodStorageUsed, SnapshotStorageUsed) publish no datapoints for non-Aurora instances — verified against this account, dimensioned and not. Actual backup bytes are a billing-only figure, via Cost Explorer. The step up when the volume autoscales is the growth signal to watch.

panels.title: Manual snapshot in progress
panels.description: PercentProgress of each manual snapshot over its first 12 hours, such as the final snapshot the destroy workflow takes before deleting a colour. 'Backup in progress' above covers automated snapshots only, because those are what a restore selects. Read from the inventory Lambda's rds_snapshot lines rather than a metric, so it also covers a snapshot whose instance is already gone. The Lambda polls every 5 minutes, so a snapshot that finishes faster shows one bar. The 12-hour cutoff stops a retained snapshot drawing 100% indefinitely.

targets.expression:
parse @message /rds_snapshot\|(?<instance>[^|]*)\|(?<snapshot>[^|]*)\|(?<r_type>[^|]*)\|(?<r_status>[^|]*)\|(?<r_created>[^|]*)\|(?<r_age>[^|]*)\|(?<r_volume>[^|]*)\|(?<r_progress>[^|]*)/
| filter r_type = "manual" and r_age <= 12
| stats max(r_progress) as progress by bin(5m), snapshot

panels.title: Snapshots that exist
panels.description: Every snapshot the inventory Lambda saw over the dashboard's time range, one row each — automated and manual, unlike the metrics above, which track automated only. A destroyed colour's final snapshot, the one kept for DR, stays listed under its instance after the instance is gone. The Lambda logs the whole list every 5 minutes, so rows are collapsed to the newest sighting per snapshot with `stats latest(...) by instance, snapshot`; without that the table repeats each snapshot once per poll. At the default now-1h that is exactly the current inventory; widen the range to see snapshots that have since aged out of retention. `volume_gib` is the instance's allocated storage at snapshot time, not the snapshot's own size. The aggregated columns are parsed into `r_*` names and renamed by `stats`, because aliasing `latest(type) as type` over a field `parse` already defined is rejected with `Ephemeral field is already defined`; `instance` and `snapshot` keep their names only because the `by` clause never re-defines them.

targets.expression:
fields @timestamp
| parse @message /rds_snapshot\|(?<instance>[^|]*)\|(?<snapshot>[^|]*)\|(?<r_type>[^|]*)\|(?<r_status>[^|]*)\|(?<r_created>[^|]*)\|(?<r_age>[^|]*)\|(?<r_volume>[^|]*)\|(?<r_progress>[^|]*)/
| filter ispresent(snapshot)
| stats latest(r_type) as type, latest(r_status) as status, latest(r_created) as created, latest(r_age) as age_hours, latest(r_volume) as volume_gib, latest(r_progress) as progress by instance, snapshot
| sort created desc
| limit 200

panels.title: Volume initialized
panels.description: RDS's own StorageOperationPercentProgress per instance, published as VeWorld/RDSBackups StorageInitialized by the backup inventory Lambda every 5 minutes. A restored volume is 'Initializing' until every block has come down from its snapshot; 100 means RDS has finished, so no read waits on S3 any more. It counts the prewarm's reads and RDS's own background loading together. RDS moves it in steps of several percent, roughly every 10 minutes, so a flat stretch is not a stall.

panels.title: Prewarm runs — last 7 days
panels.description: One row per pg_prewarm task, parsed from the prewarm_total / prewarm_range / prewarm_done lines terraform/api/scripts/pg_prewarm.sh prints. A restored instance fetches every block from its snapshot on first read, so until Percent reaches 100 the indexers pay that fetch on any page the sweep has not reached. Done is 1 once the sweep finished; a run with Done 0 and a stale Last line stopped early — its exit code is in the task's ECS events. Runs from before the chunked script print none of these lines and do not appear. One query per colour, so a destroyed colour's missing log group errors its half only.

targets.expression:
fields @timestamp
| parse @log /prod-(?<colour>[a-z]+)-pg-prewarm/
| parse @logStream /^(?<net>[^\/]+)\/psql\/(?<task>.+)$/
| parse @message /^prewarm_total\|(?<r_ranges>\d+)\|(?<r_pages>\d+)$/
| parse @message /^prewarm_range\|[^|]*\|\d+\|(?<r_warmed>\d+)$/
| parse @message /^(?<r_done>prewarm_done)$/
| filter ispresent(r_ranges) or ispresent(r_warmed) or ispresent(r_done)
| stats min(@timestamp) as started, max(@timestamp) as last_line, max(r_pages) * 8 / 1048576 as total_gib, sum(r_warmed) * 8 / 1048576 as warmed_gib, 100 * sum(r_warmed) / max(r_pages) as percent, count(r_warmed) as ranges_done, max(r_ranges) as ranges, count(r_done) as finished by colour, net, task
| sort started desc

fields @timestamp
| parse @log /prod-(?<colour>[a-z]+)-pg-prewarm/
| parse @logStream /^(?<net>[^\/]+)\/psql\/(?<task>.+)$/
| parse @message /^prewarm_total\|(?<r_ranges>\d+)\|(?<r_pages>\d+)$/
| parse @message /^prewarm_range\|[^|]*\|\d+\|(?<r_warmed>\d+)$/
| parse @message /^(?<r_done>prewarm_done)$/
| filter ispresent(r_ranges) or ispresent(r_warmed) or ispresent(r_done)
| stats min(@timestamp) as started, max(@timestamp) as last_line, max(r_pages) * 8 / 1048576 as total_gib, sum(r_warmed) * 8 / 1048576 as warmed_gib, 100 * sum(r_warmed) / max(r_pages) as percent, count(r_warmed) as ranges_done, max(r_ranges) as ranges, count(r_done) as finished by colour, net, task
| sort started desc

panels.title: Prewarm read rate
panels.description: MiB/s the prewarm read, per colour and network, from the pages each 1 GiB range reports in 5-minute bins. postgres.prewarm_parallelism in terraform/api/environments/*.yml sets how many ranges run at once; each session reads at roughly 8 MiB/s against a cold volume, so this scales with it until the instance class's EBS bandwidth does not.

targets.expression:
parse @log /prod-(?<colour>[a-z]+)-pg-prewarm/
| parse @logStream /^(?<net>[^\/]+)\//
| parse @message /^prewarm_range\|[^|]*\|\d+\|(?<r_warmed>\d+)$/
| filter ispresent(r_warmed)
| stats sum(r_warmed) * 8 / 1024 / 300 as mib_per_s by bin(5m), colour, net

parse @log /prod-(?<colour>[a-z]+)-pg-prewarm/
| parse @logStream /^(?<net>[^\/]+)\//
| parse @message /^prewarm_range\|[^|]*\|\d+\|(?<r_warmed>\d+)$/
| filter ispresent(r_warmed)
| stats sum(r_warmed) * 8 / 1024 / 300 as mib_per_s by bin(5m), colour, net

panels.title: Read latency
panels.description: AWS/RDS ReadLatency per instance: the cold-volume signal the prewarm exists to clear. Around 40-50 ms per read while blocks still come from the snapshot, against ~1 ms once warm. It falls as the sweep covers the pages the indexers read, well before Percent reaches 100.

panels.title: WAF request detail · Mainnet — Logs Insights, runs only while expanded
Flagged traffic over the range
panels.description: The denominator for the two tables below, from the WAF log group in us-east-1 (CLOUDFRONT-scope ACLs log there, not eu-west-1). This group carries BLOCKed requests only — logging_filter_block_only is on for mainnet — so it is a rejection census, not a traffic one; total edge volume is 'CloudFront requests' in the Edge · Mainnet row. Where clients and paths run to thousands, the top 20 rows below are the head of a long tail rather than its bulk.

targets.expression:
filter terminatingRuleId != "Default_Action" or ispresent(nonTerminatingMatchingRules.0.ruleId)
| stats count(*) as flagged, count_distinct(httpRequest.clientIp) as clients, count_distinct(httpRequest.uri) as paths

panels.title: Flagged clients
panels.description: Who tripped a rule, by source IP. `flagged` counts that client's matched requests, never its whole traffic. `rule` is the WebACL rule name, the same vocabulary as the Rule dimension in 'WAF — blocked requests by rule'. `action` reads BLOCK throughout while no rule runs in Count mode (the managed groups use override_action none); ALLOW would mean a count-mode dry run that was still served. A cloud scraper spreads itself over a range, so one actor arrives here as many small rows — the totals above are its real size.

targets.expression:
fields httpRequest.clientIp as clientIp, httpRequest.country as country, httpRequest.uri as path, coalesce(nonTerminatingMatchingRules.0.ruleId, terminatingRuleId, labels.0.name) as rule
| filter terminatingRuleId != "Default_Action" or ispresent(nonTerminatingMatchingRules.0.ruleId)
| stats count(*) as flagged, count_distinct(path) as paths, count_distinct(rule) as rules by clientIp, country, action
| sort flagged desc
| limit 20

panels.title: Flagged paths
panels.description: What those requests asked for. Indexer API routes mean real callers behind a flagged IP range; probe paths — wp-login, .env, phpmyadmin — mean the rule is earning its place. `clients` is how many distinct sources asked for that path. Paths are full request URIs, so one endpoint spreads across many rows here where 'Top URIs by total requests' collapses it into one Spring pattern.

targets.expression:
fields httpRequest.uri as path, httpRequest.httpMethod as method, httpRequest.clientIp as clientIp, coalesce(nonTerminatingMatchingRules.0.ruleId, terminatingRuleId, labels.0.name) as rule
| filter terminatingRuleId != "Default_Action" or ispresent(nonTerminatingMatchingRules.0.ruleId)
| stats count(*) as flagged, count_distinct(clientIp) as clients by path, method, rule
| sort flagged desc
| limit 20
